title: Older-Adult Fall Risk: Review the Medicines, Not Just the Floor
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Falls in older adults are often multifactorial. Medication effects such as sedation, orthostasis, blurred vision, hypoglycemia, and slowed reaction time should be reviewed along with gait, footwear, environment, and sensory deficits.
recognize: Recent falls, dizziness, sleep medicines, anxiolytics, antihypertensives, opioids, diabetes therapy, and multiple medications increase risk.
priorities: Identify fall-risk symptoms and communicate medication concerns for pharmacist/prescriber review rather than independently stopping therapy.
assessMonitor: Falls/near-falls, orthostatic symptoms, gait/balance, vision, cognition, medication list including OTC/herbals, and adherence.
interventions: Implement mobility/environment precautions and coordinate medication review.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly discontinue high-risk medications without an authorized plan; deprescribing may require tapering and indication review.
teaching: Ask a clinician/pharmacist to review medicines that cause dizziness or sleepiness.
delegationScope: Fall-risk observations may be delegated; medication-risk interpretation and care-plan changes require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Adding only a bed alarm without reviewing new sedating medication after recurrent falls.
oneLinePearl: A fall-risk assessment that ignores medications is incomplete.

title: Polypharmacy: Count Prescriptions, OTCs, Supplements, and Duplicate Ingredients
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Medication reconciliation in older adults must include prescriptions, OTC medicines, vitamins, herbals, as-needed products, duplicate brands, recent discharges, and medications from multiple prescribers/pharmacies.
recognize: Duplicate ingredients, old prescriptions still taken, multiple dose strengths, and different lists across care settings are common hazards.
priorities: Build one actual-use list and clarify discrepancies with pharmacy/prescribers.
assessMonitor: What is actually taken, dose/timing, indication, prescriber, pharmacy, adherence, renal/hepatic changes, side effects and recent hospital changes.
interventions: Use teach-back and an updated written list; remove obsolete list entries only through approved reconciliation workflow.
medicationSafety: Never assume the electronic medication list equals actual use.
teaching: Bring all medicines and supplements or a complete list to every transition of care.
delegationScope: Medication history collection may be assisted, but reconciliation/discrepancy resolution requires licensed clinical oversight.
examTrap: Reconciling only prescription medications from the current clinic list.
oneLinePearl: The safest medication list is the one that matches what the patient actually takes.
sourceBasis: CDC medicines risk resources for older adults

title: New Confusion After a Medication Change: Think Adverse Drug Effect and Delirium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Abrupt confusion after starting or increasing a medication should trigger evaluation for delirium and adverse drug effects along with infection, hypoxia, pain, retention, dehydration, and metabolic causes. Do not attribute the change to normal aging.
recognize: Sedatives, opioids, anticholinergics, polypharmacy, renal decline, and drug interactions can precipitate acute cognitive change.
priorities: Compare with baseline, assess physiologic causes and recent medication changes, and notify the RN/provider promptly.
assessMonitor: Onset/fluctuation, attention, vital signs, oxygenation, glucose as indicated, hydration, pain, urinary/stool retention, medication timing and renal function.
interventions: Reduce environmental triggers, support orientation, mobility/sensory aids, and follow the medication/medical evaluation plan.
medicationSafety: Do not add a sedative simply to suppress agitation before evaluating the cause.
teaching: Families should report abrupt cognitive changes and recent medication changes.
delegationScope: Behavior observations may be delegated; interpretation of acute confusion requires licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Calling new confusion dementia because the client is older.
oneLinePearl: Acute confusion is a change to explain, not an age to accept.

title: Older Adult on Anticoagulants After a Fall: Head Injury Risk Can Be Hidden
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A fall or head impact in an older adult taking anticoagulants requires careful evaluation even if symptoms seem mild. Delayed intracranial bleeding can occur and medication history must be communicated immediately.
recognize: Headache, vomiting, confusion, somnolence, weakness, unequal pupils, gait change, or any loss of consciousness are high-risk cues.
priorities: Assess neurologic status and mechanism, identify anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy and last dose, and escalate according to trauma protocol.
assessMonitor: Neuro checks, vital signs, pain, bruising/bleeding, medication timing, and baseline cognition.
interventions: Use fall/bleeding precautions and emergency imaging/evaluation pathway as ordered.
medicationSafety: Do not independently administer reversal agents or hold anticoagulation without authorized plan unless emergency protocol explicitly directs.
teaching: Seek prompt evaluation after significant head injury while taking blood thinners, even if initially feeling well.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be shared; head-injury and anticoagulant risk interpretation require licensed escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring a fully alert anticoagulated older adult after a head strike without further evaluation.

oneLinePearl: Blood thinners make a seemingly minor head fall a higher-risk event.
sourceBasis: CDC medication safety data noting anticoagulant ADE burden

title: Older-Adult Hypoglycemia: Medication Harm May Present as Confusion or a Fall
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Insulin and other glucose-lowering therapy can cause hypoglycemia that presents atypically in older adults—confusion, weakness, dizziness, fall, behavior change, or somnolence. Check glucose promptly when clinically indicated.
recognize: Poor intake, renal decline, medication duplication, changed meal pattern, recent illness, or intensified therapy increase risk.
priorities: Check glucose and treat per hypoglycemia protocol while assessing airway/safety and cause.
assessMonitor: Glucose trend, intake, medication timing, renal function, cognition, falls and recurrence.
interventions: Use the ordered hypoglycemia treatment and reassess response; notify the diabetes/prescribing team for recurrent episodes.
medicationSafety: Do not simply resume the same regimen after recurrent hypoglycemia without review.
teaching: Recognize individual hypoglycemia symptoms and keep a treatment/medication plan current.
delegationScope: Glucose testing may be delegated when trained; treatment and regimen changes follow protocol/licensed oversight.
examTrap: Assuming new confusion is dementia without checking glucose in a client on insulin.
oneLinePearl: In an older adult on glucose-lowering therapy, confusion or a fall may be hypoglycemia until checked.

title: Renal Decline Changes Medication Exposure in Older Adults
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Declining kidney function can increase exposure to renally cleared medications and active metabolites. New sedation, confusion, bleeding, hypoglycemia, or other toxicity after illness or renal decline requires medication review.
recognize: Dehydration, AKI, infection, diuretics, nephrotoxic drugs, and chronic kidney disease can change clearance quickly.
priorities: Review recent creatinine/eGFR trends as ordered, medication list, doses and toxicity cues; notify prescriber/pharmacy for adjustment assessment.
assessMonitor: Renal labs, intake/output, weight/hydration, medication effects and adverse events.
interventions: Support hydration/renal plan and medication reconciliation.
medicationSafety: Do not independently reduce doses; dosing depends on medication-specific renal guidance and clinical indication.
teaching: Report new illness/dehydration and ask whether medications need review when kidney function changes.
delegationScope: I/O may be delegated; renal dose assessment requires licensed pharmacy/prescriber review.
examTrap: Continuing all chronic doses unchanged after acute renal deterioration without review.
oneLinePearl: When kidneys slow down, some drugs effectively speed up.

title: Orthostatic Symptoms: Connect Dizziness With Medication Timing and Hydration
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Dizziness on standing may reflect volume depletion, autonomic disease, or medication effects. In older adults, review antihypertensives, diuretics, sedatives and other fall-risk medicines while assessing hydration and orthostatic findings.
recognize: Symptoms after medication dosing, illness, poor intake, or dose escalation increase suspicion for treatment-related hypotension.
priorities: Prevent falls, obtain ordered orthostatic measurements, and communicate medication/hydration patterns for review.
assessMonitor: Symptoms, BP/HR position changes, hydration, recent dose changes, gait and fall history.
interventions: Assist position changes slowly, ensure mobility support, and follow hydration/medication plan.
medicationSafety: Do not advise the patient to stop antihypertensive therapy independently.
teaching: Rise slowly, use prescribed supports, and report recurrent dizziness or falls.
delegationScope: Orthostatic measurement may be delegated if trained; interpretation and medication changes require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Treating every fall as an environmental issue when symptoms began after a medication increase.
oneLinePearl: Ask when the dizziness happens and when the medicines were taken.

title: High-Risk Adverse Drug Events: Anticoagulants, Diabetes Agents, and Antibiotics Deserve Vigilance
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Older adults have a high burden of emergency visits for adverse drug events. Anticoagulants, diabetes agents, and antibiotics are prominent contributors, so new bleeding, hypoglycemia, allergy, diarrhea, renal change, or confusion should trigger medication review.
recognize: Polypharmacy and age-related physiologic change increase vulnerability to ADEs.
priorities: Link new symptoms temporally to medications and communicate high-risk therapy during every transition.
assessMonitor: Bleeding, glucose, allergy/infection treatment response, renal/hepatic function, medication adherence and interactions.
interventions: Use drug-specific monitoring and safety protocols.
medicationSafety: Avoid prescribing-style blanket rules; identify the medication, indication, dose, monitoring and current symptom.
teaching: Keep an updated medication list and know the most important warning signs for high-risk medicines.
delegationScope: Symptom observation may be shared; ADE assessment and medication changes require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Treating a new symptom without asking whether a high-risk medication could be contributing.
oneLinePearl: Every new symptom in polypharmacy deserves a medication question.

title: Medication Effects and Driving: Drowsiness, Vision Change, and Slowed Reaction Time Matter
bottomLine: Some prescriptions, OTC medicines, supplements, and herbals can impair alertness, balance, vision, or reaction time and increase both fall and driving risk. New impairment after medication changes should prompt clinician/pharmacist review.
recognize: Sleep medicines, anxiety medicines, pain medicines and other sedating/vision-affecting therapies can reduce safe driving ability.
priorities: Identify symptoms and counsel the patient not to drive when impaired while seeking medication review.
assessMonitor: Drowsiness, dizziness, vision, reaction time, confusion, medication timing and driving/fall history.
interventions: Use medication lists and action plans to discuss risk with provider/pharmacist.
medicationSafety: OTC and herbal products count as medications for impairment risk.
teaching: Do not drive when a medicine makes you sleepy, dizzy, confused, or visually impaired.
delegationScope: Safety teaching may be reinforced; formal driving fitness determinations depend on clinician/jurisdiction.
examTrap: Ignoring OTC sleep aids because they are nonprescription.
sourceBasis: CDC Older Adult Drivers Medicines Risk Fact Sheet 2024

title: Transitions of Care: Deprescribing Requires an Intentional Handoff
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Medication changes made during hospitalization must be explicit at discharge: what stopped, what started, what changed, why, what is temporary, what needs monitoring, and what should be resumed or never resumed. Vague discontinuation creates duplication and rebound risk.
recognize: Patients often restart old bottles at home unless the change is clearly explained and reconciled.
priorities: Compare preadmission, inpatient and discharge lists and identify every unexplained discrepancy.
assessMonitor: Indication, duration, dose changes, taper plans, monitoring, pharmacy access and caregiver understanding.
interventions: Use teach-back and a single updated list; communicate with outpatient clinicians/pharmacy.
medicationSafety: Deprescribing may require tapering; never tell a patient to abruptly stop chronic therapy without the authorized plan.
redFlags: Old high-risk medication still available at home
teaching: Remove or separate discontinued medicines only after confirming the discharge plan and know which changes are temporary.
delegationScope: Teaching reinforcement may be within PN/LVN role; reconciliation and deprescribing decisions require licensed/prescriber oversight.
examTrap: Handing the patient a new list without comparing it with medications already in the home.
oneLinePearl: A medication change is not complete until the old plan is clearly closed.
